extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students studying functional analysis / Banach and Hilbert spaces
extracted.subtask_description: A compact collection of central theorems and corollaries in Banach-space theory (Hahn–Banach, Uniform Boundedness, Open Mapping, Closed Graph, reflexivity facts) together with proofs, examples, and exercises. Useful as a reference for proving existence/extension of functionals, separation results, and basic operator-theoretic consequences in functional analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension dominated by sublinear functional (Lemma 12.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be a real vector space and p a real-valued function on X satisfying the sublinear-type inequalities; if Y is a subspace and f is a linear functional on Y with f(y) ≤ p(y) for all y∈Y, then there exists a linear functional F on X extending f with F(x) ≤ p(x) for all x∈X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved via Zorn’s Lemma: consider the family of linear functionals on subspaces extending f and dominated by p, order by extension, take unions along chains to get upper bounds, choose a maximal extension f0 on Y0, and show any vector outside Y0 can be adjoined by defining values using a suitable choice of constant between a supremum and infimum. The proof constructs the one-dimensional extension explicitly and checks the domination inequality. This lemma is the key ‘real’ case ingredient for Hahn–Banach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hahn–Banach extension theorem (Theorem 12.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous linear functional defined on a subspace can be extended to the whole normed space without increasing its norm: for Y a subspace of a normed space X and y*∈Y*, there exists x*∈X* with x*|_Y = y* and ||x*|| = ||y*||. The real-scalar case follows from the lemma; the complex case is reduced to the real case by extending the real part and reconstructing a complex linear functional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lemma 12.14 with p(x)=||y*||·||x|| (or suitable p) in the real case. For complex scalars, extend Re(y*) as a real-linear functional with no increase in norm, then define x*(x)=F(x)−iF(ix) to obtain a complex-linear extension preserving norm. Proof details show how norm-preservation is checked via rotation by e^{-iθ} to kill imaginary part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of a point from a closed subspace (Corollary 12.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y is a closed subspace of a normed linear space X and x0∉Y, then there exists x*∈X* such that x*(y)=0 for all y∈Y and x*(x0)=1. Moreover, ||x*|| can be taken equal to the reciprocal of the distance from x0 to Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a bounded linear functional z* on the one-dimensional extension (span{Y,x0}) with prescribed values using the distance d and show ||z*|| = 1/d, then apply Hahn–Banach to extend to all of X without increasing norm. This gives a separating functional and a quantitative norm estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a norming functional (Corollary 12.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any x0≠0 in a normed linear space X there exists x*∈X* with ||x*|| = 1 and x*(x0) = ||x0||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A direct corollary of Corollary 12.15 by applying it to x0 scaled appropriately; shows the dual separates points and attains the norm on each nonzero vector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual norm characterization (Corollary 12.17)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from existence of a norming functional (Corollary 12.16) which attains the sup, and the evident inequality |x*(x0)| ≤ ||x*||·||x0|| gives the opposite inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical embedding into the double dual (definition and Corollary 12.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the canonical map ∂: X → X** by (∂(x))(x*) = x*(x) for all x*∈X*. Then ∂ is linear and isometric: ||∂(x)|| = ||x||. If X is complete, ∂(X) is a closed subspace of X**.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute norms via the dual sup formula (Corollary 12.17). This yields the notion of reflexivity (∂ onto X**). Examples: finite-dimensional spaces and Hilbert spaces are reflexive; L^p spaces for 1<p<∞ are reflexive (σ-finite hypothesis discussed), while L^1 and L^∞ often are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexivity facts and counterexamples (Propositions 12.19, 12.20 and Corollary 12.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (S,µ) is σ-finite and has infinitely many disjoint measurable sets of positive measure, then L^1(S,µ) is not reflexive (Prop.12.19). If X is Banach and X* is reflexive then X is reflexive (Prop.12.20). Consequently under the same measure-theoretic hypothesis L^∞(S,µ) is not reflexive (Cor.12.21).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexamples are constructed by producing continuous linear functionals on L^∞ not given by integration against an L^1 function, using Hahn–Banach to extend functionals defined on a suitable subspace. Proposition 12.20 uses the canonical maps and duality to show reflexivity of the dual forces reflexivity of X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform Boundedness Principle / Banach–Steinhaus Theorem (Theorem 12.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let {L_α} be a family of bounded linear operators from a Banach space X to a normed linear space Y. If for every x∈X the supremum sup_α ||L_α(x)|| is finite, then sup_α ||L_α|| < ∞; equivalently there is a constant C such that ||L_α|| ≤ C for all α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof employs the Baire Category Theorem: consider closed sets where operators are uniformly bounded at level n, find one containing a nonempty open set, and then deduce a uniform operator norm bound. Important applications include proving existence of continuous functions whose Fourier series do not converge at certain points by exhibiting functionals with unbounded operator norms (Lebesgue constants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unboundedness of Lebesgue constants (Proposition 12.23) — example/application
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lebesgue constants L_n = (1/2π) ∫_{-π}^{π} |D_n(t)| dt satisfy L_n = O(log n) and hence are unbounded as n→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analytic estimate (decomposing D_n and estimating integrals / Riemann sums) is used together with Uniform Boundedness to show there exists a continuous periodic function whose Fourier series diverges at some point (because boundedness of point-evaluation functionals would force bounded Lebesgue constants). The proposition provides the concrete sequence of bounded linear functionals with unbounded norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open Mapping Theorem / Interior Mapping Principle (Theorem 12.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is a continuous linear operator from a Banach space X onto a Banach space Y, then L maps open subsets of X to open subsets of Y (i.e., L is an open mapping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof proceeds in three steps: show closure of L(B1) contains a neighborhood of 0 via Baire Category, deduce images of scaled balls contain scaled neighborhoods using linearity, and then use successive approximations to represent arbitrary small y∈Y as L(x) with x small. Corollary: bijective continuous linear maps between Banach spaces have continuous inverses (bounded inverse theorem). Examples demonstrate consequences and also exhibit non-surjective continuous maps (Fourier coefficient mapping) to show where hypotheses fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded inverse theorem (Corollary 12.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-to-one continuous linear operator L between Banach spaces X and Y that maps onto Y has a continuous linear inverse L^{-1}: Y→X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from the Open Mapping Theorem: since L is open, inverse images of open sets are open, so L^{-1} is continuous. Used to deduce that injective surjective continuous linear maps between Banach spaces are isomorphisms of topological vector spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed Graph Theorem (Corollary 12.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L: X→Y is a linear operator between Banach spaces whose graph G = {(x,L(x)) : x∈X} is closed in X×Y, then L is bounded (continuous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make X×Y a Banach space with the sum norm; G is a closed linear subspace and hence Banach. The projection map P: G→X given by P((x,L(x))) = x is continuous (its inverse exists and is linear), and using bounded inverse/corollary arguments one deduces boundedness of L via composition with coordinate projections. Example: derivative operator on C^1([0,1]) has closed graph but is unbounded on larger domains if domain is not complete; the theorem requires both domain and codomain to be Banach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed graph vs continuity for linear maps (discussion / example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For general functions between metric (or Hausdorff) spaces continuity implies closed graph, but the converse need not hold. For linear operators between Banach spaces the converse does hold: closed graph ⇒ bounded (Closed Graph Theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives examples showing linearity alone is not enough (the derivative operator on the subspace of continuously differentiable functions has closed graph but is unbounded when considered as an operator from a non-complete domain), and explains why completeness of domain and codomain is essential in the theorem.
